newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. realtor sees int'l interest in HK property.
newsitem.headline: U.S. realtor sees int'l interest in HK property.

text.p: Hong Kong's soaring property prices are deterring international investors from buying here, but the territory's China link and moderating prices should ensure future interest, a U.S. realtor said on Friday.

"Prices are quite high right now so it is hard for us to attract U.S. investors or Japanese investors, but times change," Richard Mandel, managing director Asia of U.S. real estate firm Kennedy-Wilson Inc told Reuters in an interview.
"Hong Kong is really the financial centre for China."
Kennedy-Wilson formed a joint venture company earlier this month with local firm Goldman Property Consultants Ltd.
As well as marketing international properties to Asian buyers, Kennedy-Goldman (HK) Ltd will deal with office sales and leasing and residential sales in Hong Kong.

"The reason companies come to Hong Kong is because of the China factor. Hong Kong is still a financial centre and they need to have Hong Kong as a stepping stone to capture the China market," Kennedy-Goldman managing director Raymond Fung said.
Mandel said Hong Kong property prices were likely to remain at a premium to other cities in Asia, but companies would still chose to build operations here.
"They obviously believe that the productivity in Hong Kong will more than compensate for the higher costs."
Residential property prices surged by about 30 percent during the first six months of this year and office capital values gained about 30 percent in the last quarter of 1996.
Fung said office prices had held strong until about March, but government moves to curb speculation and rising real estate prices had cooled sentiment.

He said residential prices had dropped 10 percent since Hong Kong's new government announced plans to increase housing supply earlier this month and were expected to drop another 10 percent ahead of a government policy statement in October.
"I think residential prices will grow more steadily in the future," said Fung.
He said while limited supply in core locations would keep Grade-A office prices buoyant, increased supply in other areas would dampen Grade-B office prices.
"Demand will be strong because a number of PRC (People's Republic of China) companies will be coming," said Fung.

"In the coming 12 months prices will increase 10-20 percent in the core locations, but I am quite pessimistic about tertiary location office prices. They could be down around five to 10 percent for Grade-B office space," he added.
